question: A Brazilian commercial bank is establishing an internal AI governance committee. Under Brazil's PL 2338/2023, what governance structures and internal processes must AI agents put in place, and what additional measures apply once a system is high-risk?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023 Art. 19, AI agents (providers and operators) must establish governance structures and internal processes ensuring system security and the rights of affected persons, including at least: transparency measures for human-machine interaction; transparency about governance measures adopted; data-management measures to mitigate discriminatory bias; legitimation of data processing under the LGPD (privacy by design and by default, data minimization); adequate separation of training/testing/validation data; and information-security measures across the lifecycle. Art. 19(2) requires that technical documentation of high-risk systems be prepared before market availability and kept updated. For high-risk systems, Art. 20 adds: lifecycle documentation of design/implementation/use decisions; automatic operation-logging to assess accuracy, robustness, and discriminatory potential; reliability testing (robustness, accuracy, precision, coverage); bias-mitigation data-management including an inclusive design team; and technical measures enabling explainability. The bank's committee should assign ownership for each of these obligations.
notes: AI-assisted draft; [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 19/20 item wording against Senate consolidated text. BR uses agente/fornecedor/operador rather than a named committee; committee structure is inferred good practice, not a statutory body.

question: How should a Brazilian bank determine and document the risk level of a credit-scoring AI system under PL 2338/2023 before deploying it?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 13 requires that, prior to market placement or use in service, every AI system undergo a preliminary risk assessment (avaliação preliminar) performed by the provider to classify its risk degree. The assessment must be registered and documented for accountability, particularly where the system is not classified as high-risk (Art. 13(2)). For credit scoring, the preliminary assessment will identify the system as high-risk because Art. 17(V) lists 'evaluation of the debt-capacity of natural persons or establishment of their credit classification' as high-risk. The competent authority may order reclassification and an algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 13(3)); if reclassified as high-risk, the impact assessment and Chapter IV governance measures become mandatory, with penalties for fraudulent or false preliminary assessment (Art. 13(4)).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 13 paragraph numbering. Credit=high-risk confirmed in Art. 17(V) of Senate text.

question: A Brazilian financial group operates many AI systems across lending, insurance, and investment. What does PL 2338/2023 require regarding lifecycle management and documentation of these systems?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 19(1) states that governance measures apply across the entire AI lifecycle, from initial conception to discontinuation. Art. 19(2) requires technical documentation of high-risk systems to be prepared before market availability and kept updated during use. For high-risk systems, Art. 20(I) requires documentation, in a format adequate to the development process and technology used, of the system's functioning and of the decisions involved in its construction, implementation, and use, considering all relevant lifecycle stages (design, development, evaluation, operation, discontinuation). The group should maintain an inventory that distinguishes high-risk systems (e.g., credit scoring under Art. 17(V)) from lower-risk ones, since documentation and impact-assessment duties attach primarily to high-risk systems.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] paragraph numbering. Inventory framing is good practice; the statute mandates documentation, not an inventory per se.

question: What human oversight requirements does PL 2338/2023 impose on a bank operating a high-risk AI system, and what rights do affected customers have to human review?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20 sole paragraph requires that human oversight of high-risk systems enable responsible persons to: understand the system's capacities and limitations and control its functioning so anomalies can be identified and resolved quickly; be aware of automation/over-reliance bias; correctly interpret outputs; decide in any specific situation not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output; and intervene in or interrupt operation. On the rights side, Art. 10 gives affected persons the right to request human intervention or review where an AI decision produces relevant legal effects or significantly affects their interests, including through profiling. Art. 11 requires significant human involvement and a final human determination where impacts are irreversible or hard to reverse, or involve risks to life or physical integrity. For lending, this means a human must be able to review and override adverse credit decisions.
legal_basis: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20 sole paragraph; Art. 10; Art. 11
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] sole-paragraph item numbering (I-V).

question: Does PL 2338/2023 require staff training or awareness measures for AI systems, and what form do they take?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 addresses training and awareness primarily within the algorithmic impact assessment. Art. 24(1)(g) requires the impact assessment to record training and awareness actions concerning the risks associated with the AI system. Additionally, Art. 20(IV)(b) requires, as a bias-mitigation data-management measure for high-risk systems, an inclusive design and development team oriented toward diversity, which implies competence and awareness requirements for those building the system. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, PL 2338 does not prescribe an organization-wide training program in detail; training obligations are framed through the impact-assessment and governance measures rather than as a standalone requirement.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 24 sub-item lettering. Contrast-with-NIST note is interpretive.

question: A Brazilian bank uses a vendor-supplied credit-scoring model. Under PL 2338/2023, how are responsibilities split between the vendor and the bank, and who is liable for harm?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 4 distinguishes the fornecedor (provider) — who develops the system to place it on the market — from the operador (operator) — who uses the system in its own name or benefit. A bank using a vendor credit-scoring model is the operador. Both are 'agentes de IA' and share governance duties under Arts. 19-20 to the extent of their role. On liability, Art. 27 provides that a provider or operator causing patrimonial, moral, individual, or collective damage must fully repair it regardless of the system's autonomy; Art. 27(1) imposes strict (objective) liability on the provider or operator of a high-risk system, to the extent of each one's participation in the harm. Because credit scoring is high-risk (Art. 17(V)), the bank faces strict liability for damages arising from its operation of the model, alongside the vendor.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] strict-liability scope (Art. 27 §1) and operador/fornecedor split before relying on this in evaluation.

question: A Brazilian bank plans to deploy an AI-based credit-scoring system for personal loans. How is this system classified under PL 2338/2023, and what is the legal basis?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023 Art. 17(V), AI systems used for 'evaluation of the debt-capacity of natural persons or establishment of their credit classification' (avaliação da capacidade de endividamento das pessoas naturais ou estabelecimento de sua classificação de crédito) are expressly classified as high-risk (alto risco). A personal-loan credit-scoring system falls squarely within this category. High-risk classification triggers the mandatory governance measures of Arts. 19-20, a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22), strict civil liability (Art. 27(1)), and the affected-person rights of Chapter II (information, explanation, contestation, human review). This mirrors the EU AI Act (Annex III, Art. 5(b)) and the Korean AI Basic Act (Art. 2(4)) treatment of credit AI as their highest regulated tier.
notes: Core financial provision; Art. 17(V) confirmed in Senate consolidated text.

question: An insurance subsidiary uses AI to price life insurance premiums from health and lifestyle data. Is this high-risk under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not explicitly list insurance pricing in its high-risk catalogue (Art. 17), which is a notable divergence from the EU AI Act (which expressly lists life and health insurance pricing as high-risk under Annex III, Art. 5(c)). Life-insurance pricing is therefore not automatically high-risk under the Brazilian bill's enumerated list. However, it may fall within Art. 17(IV) — 'evaluation of access, eligibility, granting, review, reduction, or revocation of essential private and public services' — if the pricing determines access to an essential service, which would require case-specific analysis. Alternatively, Art. 18 empowers the competent authority to add systems to the high-risk list based on criteria such as scale, potential for harm, and effect on vulnerable groups, so insurance-pricing AI could be designated high-risk in the future. The correct answer notes the explicit-listing gap and the two routes (Art. 17(IV) essential-services and Art. 18 authority designation).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] whether insurance is intended under Art. 17(IV) essential services — this is interpretive and a genuine BR/EU divergence worth flagging in the paper.

question: The bank deploys an AI fraud-detection system that can block transactions in real time. How is it classified under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Financial fraud detection is not enumerated among the high-risk purposes in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17. It is therefore not automatically high-risk under the Brazilian bill's list. The provider must still perform and document a preliminary risk assessment under Art. 13, which for a non-high-risk system must be registered for accountability (Art. 13(2)). The competent authority retains power under Art. 18 to designate additional high-risk categories if criteria such as scale, potential for harm, or effect on vulnerable groups are met. This treatment parallels the EU AI Act, which expressly excludes fraud detection from the credit high-risk category (Annex III, Art. 5(b)). Note that if the system produces decisions with relevant legal effects on customers (e.g., blocking accounts), the affected-person rights in Chapter II (information, contestation, human review) may still apply regardless of high-risk status.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Fraud not listed in Art. 17 — parallels EU exclusion. Chapter II rights may still attach.

question: A securities subsidiary uses an AI algorithm for automated portfolio-rebalancing recommendations to retail investors. How does PL 2338/2023 apply?
ground_truth: Automated investment/portfolio-recommendation AI is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, so it is not automatically high-risk under the bill. A preliminary risk assessment under Art. 13 is nonetheless required and must be documented. Because the recommendations affect retail investors' interests, the affected-person rights of Chapter II apply: the right to prior information about the automated nature of the interaction (Art. 5(I), Art. 7), the right to explanation of the recommendation (Art. 8), and the right to contest and request human review (Arts. 9-10) where the recommendation significantly affects the person's interests. This treatment is similar to the EU and Korean frameworks, which do not currently classify robo-advisory as high-risk/high-impact but subject it to transparency duties.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Investment not listed as high-risk; Chapter II rights apply.

question: What performance and reliability testing must a Brazilian bank conduct for its high-risk credit-scoring AI under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20(III) requires, for high-risk systems, reliability testing appropriate to the sector and type of application, including tests of robustness, accuracy, precision, and coverage (testes de robustez, acurácia, precisão e cobertura). Art. 20(II) requires automatic operation-logging tools that permit assessment of accuracy and robustness and detection of discriminatory potential, together with implementation of risk-mitigation measures with special attention to adverse effects. For a credit-scoring system, this means the bank must test the model's predictive accuracy and robustness, log its operation to enable ongoing accuracy/bias assessment, and document mitigation measures. These duties parallel EU AI Act Art. 15 (accuracy, robustness) and the logging duty in Art. 12.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 20 item numbering (II, III).

question: Before deploying a new loan-origination AI, what testing and assessment must be completed under PL 2338/2023 to demonstrate the system is safe and reliable?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023, before deployment of a high-risk loan-origination AI the bank must: (1) perform and document a preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13), which will identify the system as high-risk under Art. 17(V); (2) conduct reliability testing including robustness, accuracy, precision, and coverage appropriate to the application (Art. 20(III)); (3) implement automatic operation-logging and bias-detection measures (Art. 20(II)); and (4) carry out a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22), whose methodology (Art. 24) includes risk cognition, mitigation, and monitoring, and records test and evaluation results for rights impacts, especially discriminatory ones. Art. 19(2) requires technical documentation to be prepared before market availability. Together these constitute the pre-deployment safety and reliability demonstration.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] cross-references Art. 22/24.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 require a Brazilian bank to make its credit-scoring AI explainable, and what can a rejected loan applicant demand?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 provides two complementary explainability requirements. On the governance side, Art. 20(V) requires providers/operators of high-risk systems to adopt technical measures enabling explainability of results and to make available general information on the model's functioning, logic, and relevant criteria, and — upon request — adequate information allowing interpretation of concrete results, respecting industrial and commercial secrecy. On the rights side, Art. 8 gives an affected person (e.g., a rejected applicant) the right to request an explanation of the specific decision, including the rationale and logic, the degree of the AI's contribution, the data processed and its source, the decision criteria and their weighting as applied to the person, the mechanisms to contest, and the possibility of human intervention. This must be provided free of charge, in accessible language, within fifteen (15) days (extendable once).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] 15-day deadline and Art. 20(V) wording.

question: What ongoing monitoring obligations apply to a high-risk credit AI after deployment under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 25 establishes that the algorithmic impact assessment is a continuous iterative process executed throughout the entire lifecycle of high-risk AI systems, requiring periodic updates; the competent authority regulates update periodicity (Art. 25(1)) and updates include public participation (Art. 25(2)). Art. 24(1)(h) requires recording mitigation measures and residual-risk justification accompanied by frequent quality-control tests. Art. 24(5) requires that agents who, after deployment, become aware of unexpected risk to natural persons' rights immediately notify the competent authority and affected persons. Art. 20(II)'s automatic operation-logging supports this ongoing monitoring. For a credit AI, the bank must continuously monitor for accuracy degradation and emergent discriminatory effects and update its impact assessment.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 24/25 paragraph and sub-item references.

question: Does PL 2338/2023 require independent assessment of high-risk AI, and who must perform the algorithmic impact assessment?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 22 makes the algorithmic impact assessment mandatory whenever a system is classified as high-risk by the preliminary assessment, and requires notifying the competent authority by sharing the preliminary and impact assessments. Art. 23 requires the impact assessment to be carried out by a professional or team of professionals with the necessary technical, scientific, and legal knowledge and functional independence (independência funcional). The sole paragraph of Art. 23 empowers the competent authority to regulate cases where the assessment or its audit must necessarily be conducted by professionals external to the provider. So while internal professionals with functional independence may perform the assessment by default, external independent assessment can be required by regulation for certain cases.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] 'independência funcional' and Art. 23 sole-paragraph.

question: How must a Brazilian bank treat and mitigate identified risks in its high-risk credit AI under PL 2338/2023, and what happens if risks cannot be mitigated?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 24 sets the impact-assessment methodology, whose stages include risk cognition, mitigation of identified risks, and monitoring. Art. 24(1) requires recording, among other things, the probability and severity of adverse consequences, mitigation measures, and residual-risk justification with frequent quality-control tests, and public transparency about residual risks. Art. 24(2) invokes the precautionary principle for irreversible-impact systems. Critically, Art. 21(2) — in the context of public-power use, and instructive generally — provides that where it is impossible to eliminate or substantively mitigate the risks identified in the algorithmic impact assessment, use of the system must be discontinued. For a credit AI, the bank must implement mitigation measures, document residual risk, and, where risks to rights cannot be substantively mitigated, discontinue the system.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 21(2) applies literally to public power; its general application to private banks is interpretive.

question: What must a Brazilian bank do when a serious incident occurs with its AI system under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 31 requires AI agents to communicate to the competent authority the occurrence of serious security incidents, including where there is risk to life and physical integrity, interruption of critical-infrastructure operations, serious property or environmental damage, or serious violations of fundamental rights, in the terms of regulation. Communication must be made within a reasonable period defined by the competent authority (Art. 31(1)), and the authority verifies severity and may order corrective or mitigation measures (Art. 31(2)). Separately, Art. 24(5) requires agents who become aware of an unexpected risk to natural persons' rights after deployment to immediately notify the competent authority and affected persons. Unlike the EU AI Act Art. 73 (which specifies a 15-day window for certain incidents), PL 2338 leaves the deadline to be set by the authority.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. BR leaves deadline to regulation; contrast with EU 15-day.

question: How must residual risk be documented and disclosed for a high-risk AI system under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 24(1)(h) requires the algorithmic impact assessment to record mitigation measures and the indication and justification of the system's residual risk, accompanied by frequent quality-control tests; Art. 24(1)(i) requires public transparency about residual risks, especially where there is a high degree of harm or danger to users' health or safety. Art. 26 provides that, safeguarding industrial and commercial secrets, the conclusions of the impact assessment are public and must contain at least: a description of the intended purpose, context of use, and territorial/temporal scope; the risk-mitigation measures and the residual risk level after those measures; and a description of the participation of affected segments, if any. The bank must therefore document residual risk internally and publish the impact-assessment conclusions.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] sub-item lettering in Art. 24(1).

question: What does PL 2338/2023 require to sustain governance of an AI system over its operational life?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 19(1) provides that governance measures apply throughout the entire AI lifecycle, from initial conception to the cessation and discontinuation of activities. For high-risk systems, Art. 25 requires the algorithmic impact assessment to be a continuous iterative process across the whole lifecycle, with periodic updates whose periodicity the competent authority regulates (Art. 25(1)) and which include public participation (Art. 25(2)). The bank must therefore treat governance not as a one-time approval but as an ongoing obligation, updating documentation, testing, and impact assessments as the system and its context evolve.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: Does PL 2338/2023 require diversity or inclusion measures in the design of AI systems?
ground_truth: Yes. PL 2338/2023 Art. 20(IV)(b) requires, as a bias-mitigation data-management measure for high-risk systems, the composition of an inclusive team responsible for the conception and development of the system, oriented by the pursuit of diversity (composição de equipe inclusiva ... orientada pela busca da diversidade). This is reinforced by the principle of justice, equity, and inclusion in Art. 3(V) and non-discrimination in Art. 3(IV). Diversity of the development team is thus a concrete governance measure for high-risk systems, not merely an aspiration — distinguishing PL 2338 from frameworks that treat inclusion only as a principle.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 20(IV)(b) wording. This is a notably concrete diversity requirement.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 treat an AI system used for AML/KYC screening in a private bank?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not enumerate AML/KYC screening among the high-risk purposes in Art. 17, so a private-bank AML/KYC AI is not automatically high-risk under the bill's list. (Art. 17 does list criminal investigation and public-security risk assessment by competent authorities under items XI-XIII, but private-sector AML/KYC compliance screening is distinct.) The provider must still perform and document a preliminary risk assessment under Art. 13. The competent authority may designate additional high-risk categories under Art. 18. Where AML/KYC decisions significantly affect customers (e.g., account freezing or refusal), the Chapter II affected-person rights (information, contestation, human review) may apply. This is broadly analogous to the EU AI Act's law-enforcement exceptions leaving private AML/KYC outside the high-risk credit category.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] the public/private distinction for Art. 17(XI-XIII); interpretive.

question: Does PL 2338/2023 address the environmental impact of AI systems?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 addresses environmental concerns at the level of foundations and principles rather than as a concrete operational obligation. Art. 2(IV) lists environmental protection and sustainable development among the foundations of AI development, implementation, and use. Art. 3(I) includes inclusive growth, sustainable development, and well-being as a principle. Additionally, Art. 31's serious-incident reporting covers serious environmental damage. However, the bill does not impose specific environmental-impact measurement or disclosure obligations on AI operators comparable to a dedicated environmental-reporting regime; for a financial institution, environmental impact is a guiding principle rather than a defined compliance duty.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Environmental = principle-level, not operational duty.

question: How should a Brazilian financial group build a cross-sectoral risk profile of its AI systems under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023, each AI system must undergo a provider preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13) that classifies it into the bill's risk tiers: excessive risk / prohibited (Art. 14), high risk (Art. 17), or lower risk. For a financial group, systems used for credit/debt-capacity evaluation (Art. 17(V)) and recruitment (Art. 17(III)) are high-risk; fraud detection, robo-advisory, and AML/KYC are not enumerated and would typically be lower-risk subject to preliminary assessment. The group should map each system against Art. 17's list, document preliminary assessments (Art. 13(2)), and monitor for the Art. 18 criteria under which the competent authority may reclassify or add categories. The resulting profile drives which systems require impact assessments (Art. 22) and the enhanced Art. 20 governance measures.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] item mapping.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 apply to a robo-advisory AI serving retail investors?
ground_truth: Robo-advisory investment AI is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, so it is not automatically high-risk under the bill. It requires a documented preliminary risk assessment under Art. 13. Because it interacts with and affects retail investors, the Chapter II rights apply: prior information about the automated character of the interaction and the system's decisions (Art. 7), the right to explanation of recommendations (Art. 8), and the rights to contest and to request human review where recommendations significantly affect the person's interests (Arts. 9-10). This mirrors the EU and Korean treatment, where robo-advisory is not currently high-risk/high-impact but is subject to transparency obligations.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Consistent with cross-framework robo-advisory treatment.

question: If an insurance-pricing AI is treated as high-risk under PL 2338/2023, what validity and reliability testing applies?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not expressly list insurance pricing as high-risk (Art. 17), unlike the EU AI Act; it could be high-risk only if it falls under Art. 17(IV) essential-services access or is designated by the competent authority under Art. 18. If treated as high-risk, the Art. 20(III) reliability testing applies: tests of robustness, accuracy, precision, and coverage appropriate to the sector and application, plus Art. 20(II) automatic operation-logging to assess accuracy and robustness and detect discriminatory potential, and Art. 20(IV) bias-mitigation data-management. A mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22) would also apply. The answer should note the conditional classification: these testing duties attach only if the insurance-pricing system is classified as high-risk via Art. 17(IV) or Art. 18.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] conditional classification chain for insurance.

question: How must a Brazilian bank respond when a previously unknown risk emerges from a deployed AI system under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 24(5) requires AI agents who, after introducing a system to the market or into service, become aware of an unexpected risk to the rights of natural persons to immediately communicate the fact to the competent authority and to affected persons. For irreversible or hard-to-reverse impacts, Art. 24(2) invokes the precautionary principle, requiring the impact assessment to consider incipient, incomplete, or speculative evidence. If the emergent risk constitutes a serious incident (risk to life/physical integrity, serious rights violations, etc.), Art. 31 requires communication to the competent authority within a reasonable period, and the authority may order corrective measures. The bank must therefore notify, reassess under the precautionary principle, and mitigate or discontinue as needed.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] paragraph numbering.

question: Does PL 2338/2023 address AI literacy or public understanding, and how might it affect a bank's customer communications?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 treats AI literacy at the level of foundations: Art. 2(X) lists access to information and education, and awareness of AI systems and their applications, among the bill's foundations. Operationally, Art. 7(3) requires that AI systems directed at vulnerable groups — such as children, adolescents, the elderly, and persons with disabilities — be developed so those persons can understand the system's functioning and their rights vis-à-vis AI agents. For a bank, this means customer-facing AI (and its disclosures under Art. 7) must be intelligible, with special care for vulnerable customers. The bill does not, however, mandate a general AI-literacy training program comparable to a dedicated literacy obligation.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 7(3) vulnerable-groups wording.

category: AI Risk Context — Customer Advisory Chatbot
question: A Brazilian bank deploys a customer-service chatbot. What does PL 2338/2023 require regarding disclosure that the customer is interacting with AI?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 5(I) grants affected persons the right to prior information about their interactions with AI systems. Art. 7(1) specifies that information about the automated character of the interaction must be provided, and — beyond complete information in physical or open-digital form — also using easily recognizable icons or symbols where applicable. Art. 19(I) requires, as a general governance measure, transparency about the use of AI in interactions with natural persons, including adequate, sufficiently clear, and informative human-machine interfaces. A customer-service chatbot is not high-risk under Art. 17, but the bank must clearly disclose that the customer is interacting with an AI system. This parallels EU AI Act Art. 50 and Korean AI Basic Act Art. 31 transparency duties.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 7(1) icon/symbol provision.

question: What approval workflow does PL 2338/2023 imply for a bank reviewing a new AI system before deployment?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 implies a staged workflow: (1) the provider conducts a preliminary risk assessment classifying the system's risk degree, which must be registered and documented (Art. 13); (2) if the preliminary assessment classifies the system as high-risk, a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment is triggered (Art. 22), to be performed by qualified, functionally independent professionals (Art. 23); (3) the competent authority is notified through sharing of the preliminary and impact assessments (Art. 22 sole paragraph); and (4) the impact-assessment conclusions are made public, safeguarding trade secrets (Art. 26). A bank's internal review committee should mirror this: preliminary classification, impact assessment for high-risk systems, authority notification, and publication of conclusions.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Committee is good practice; statute specifies the assessment steps.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 treat voluntary governance programs and codes of good practice, and what benefit do they confer?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 30 allows AI agents, individually or through associations, to formulate codes of good practice and governance setting out organization, procedures, complaint-handling, security standards, and risk-mitigation measures. Art. 30(2) provides that developers and operators may implement a governance program that, at minimum, demonstrates commitment to compliance and non-maleficence, is adapted to the scale and harm potential of operations, aims to build trust with affected persons, is integrated into the general governance structure with internal and external oversight, includes response plans to reverse harmful outcomes, and is continuously updated based on monitoring. Critically, Art. 30(3) provides that voluntary adherence to a code of good practice and governance can be considered an indicator of good faith and will be taken into account by the competent authority when applying administrative sanctions. Effective governance thus has a concrete mitigating effect on penalties.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 30 paragraph numbering. Good-faith mitigation is a notable BR feature.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 prioritize AI risks across its tiers, and where do financial AI systems fall?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 establishes a tiered risk model: excessive risk / prohibited (Art. 14) at the top, high risk (Art. 17) subject to enhanced obligations, and lower risk subject only to preliminary assessment and general governance. Art. 14 prohibits subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and public-power universal social scoring. Art. 17 lists high-risk purposes, of which credit/debt-capacity evaluation (item V) and recruitment (item III) are the financial-relevant ones. Art. 18 lets the competent authority add categories based on scale, harm potential, vulnerable-group effect, irreversibility, and transparency criteria. Financial institutions should prioritize their credit-scoring and recruitment AI as high-risk, treat fraud/robo-advisory/AML as lower-risk pending preliminary assessment, and monitor Art. 18 for reclassification.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 envisage coordination between AI governance and existing financial-sector regulation in Brazil?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 34 requires the competent authority and the public bodies responsible for regulating specific economic and governmental sectors to coordinate their activities to ensure compliance with the Law. Art. 34(1) establishes a permanent communication forum, including technical cooperation, between the AI competent authority and sectoral regulators, to facilitate their regulatory, supervisory, and sanctioning powers. Art. 34(2) provides that in regulatory sandboxes involving AI conducted by sectoral regulators, the AI competent authority is notified and may comment on compliance. Art. 32 (sole paragraph, item VII) also tasks the competent authority with articulating with sectoral regulators. For a Brazilian financial institution, this means AI governance obligations under PL 2338 are intended to be coordinated with, not duplicative of, Central Bank and financial-sector supervision — analogous in spirit to the EU AI Act Art. 9(10) financial-sector integration clause.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 32 item numbering; sectoral-coordination analogy to EU Art. 9(10) is interpretive.

question: What documentation must a Brazilian bank maintain for its AI systems under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 19(2) requires that technical documentation of high-risk AI systems be prepared before the system is made available on the market or used for service provision, and kept updated during its use. For high-risk systems, Art. 20(I) requires documentation, in a format adequate to the development process and technology, of the system's functioning and of the decisions involved in its construction, implementation, and use, covering all relevant lifecycle stages (design, development, evaluation, operation, discontinuation). For lower-risk systems, Art. 13(2) requires the preliminary risk assessment to be registered and documented for accountability. A bank must therefore maintain lifecycle technical documentation for high-risk systems (e.g., credit scoring) and documented preliminary assessments for others.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does a provider categorize a general AI system's risk under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 13 requires every AI system, prior to market placement or use in service, to undergo a preliminary assessment by the provider to classify its risk degree, with the classification registered per the criteria of Chapter III. General-purpose AI providers must include in the preliminary assessment the indicated purposes or applications (Art. 13(1), referencing Art. 17 on general-purpose AI). Where the system is not classified as high-risk, the preliminary assessment is documented for accountability (Art. 13(2)). The competent authority may reclassify and require an impact assessment (Art. 13(3)), and reclassification to high-risk makes the impact assessment and Chapter IV measures mandatory (Art. 13(4)). Categorization thus rests initially on provider self-assessment against Arts. 14 and 17, subject to authority oversight.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 13(1) general-purpose reference to Art. 17.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 define and require trustworthiness (validity and reliability) for a high-risk credit AI?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 anchors trustworthiness in Art. 3(VII), which establishes reliability and robustness of AI systems and information security as a principle. Operationally, for high-risk systems Art. 20(III) requires reliability testing appropriate to the sector and application, including robustness, accuracy, precision, and coverage; Art. 20(II) requires automatic operation-logging to assess accuracy and robustness and detect discriminatory potential; and Art. 20(V) requires explainability measures. For a high-risk credit AI, demonstrating validity and reliability means documented testing of predictive accuracy and robustness, operational logging enabling ongoing evaluation, bias detection and mitigation (Art. 20(IV)), and explainability of results. These duties collectively parallel EU AI Act Art. 15 (accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What information must a Brazilian bank share with the competent authority or the public under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 requires several disclosures. Art. 22 sole paragraph requires notifying the competent authority about a high-risk system by sharing the preliminary and algorithmic impact assessments. Art. 26 requires that the conclusions of the impact assessment be public (safeguarding trade secrets), including intended purpose, mitigation measures and residual risk, and affected-segment participation. Art. 43 tasks the competent authority with creating and maintaining a public database of high-risk AI impact-assessment documents. Additionally, serious incidents must be communicated to the authority under Art. 31. A bank operating high-risk credit AI must therefore notify the authority of the system, publish impact-assessment conclusions, and report serious incidents.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 43 public-database provision.

category: AI Risk Context — Internal HR AI
question: A Brazilian bank uses AI to screen and evaluate job candidates internally. How is this classified under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023 Art. 17(III), AI systems used for 'recruitment, screening, filtering, evaluation of candidates, decisions on promotions or termination of employment contracts, task allocation, and performance and behavior evaluation' in employment and worker management are classified as high-risk. A bank's internal HR AI for candidate screening and evaluation therefore falls within the high-risk tier, triggering the Art. 19-20 governance measures, the mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22), strict liability (Art. 27(1)), and the affected-person rights of Chapter II (including explanation and human review for affected candidates and employees). This aligns with the EU AI Act (Annex III recruitment) and Korean AI Basic Act (recruitment as High-Impact).
notes: Recruitment=high-risk confirmed in Art. 17(III).

question: Does PL 2338/2023 require assessment of an AI system's benefits, not just its risks?
ground_truth: Yes. PL 2338/2023 Art. 24(1)(b) requires the algorithmic impact assessment to consider and record the benefits associated with the AI system, alongside its risks. The methodology (Art. 24) balances known and foreseeable risks (Art. 24(1)(a)) against benefits (Art. 24(1)(b)) and weighs the probability and severity of adverse consequences (Art. 24(1)(c)(d)). For a financial institution, this means the impact assessment of a high-risk system must document not only harms and mitigations but also the system's benefits, supporting a proportionality analysis consistent with the Art. 3(XII) principle of proportionality.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 24(1) sub-item lettering.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 ensure that testing and evaluation of high-risk AI is effective?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 ties testing effectiveness to both governance measures and the impact-assessment methodology. Art. 20(III) requires reliability testing (robustness, accuracy, precision, coverage) appropriate to the sector and application. Art. 24 structures the impact assessment into preparation, risk cognition, mitigation, and monitoring, and Art. 24(1)(f) requires recording the process and results of tests and evaluations and the mitigation measures taken to verify possible rights impacts, with special emphasis on potential discriminatory impacts. Art. 24(1)(h) requires residual-risk justification accompanied by frequent quality-control tests. Effectiveness is thus ensured by requiring documented, sector-appropriate testing feeding into a continuous, monitored impact assessment (Art. 25).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 24(1) sub-items.

question: How should a Brazilian insurer treat and mitigate risks in an AI underwriting system under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not expressly enumerate insurance underwriting/pricing as high-risk in Art. 17; it becomes high-risk only if it falls under Art. 17(IV) (access to essential services) or is designated by the competent authority under Art. 18. If high-risk, the insurer must treat risks through the Art. 24 impact-assessment methodology — risk cognition, mitigation, monitoring — recording adverse-consequence probability and severity, mitigation measures, and residual-risk justification (Art. 24(1)), with public transparency about residual risks. Bias-mitigation data-management (Art. 20(IV)) and the precautionary principle for irreversible impacts (Art. 24(2)) apply. If risks to rights cannot be substantively mitigated, discontinuation follows the logic of Art. 21(2). The answer should flag that these duties are conditional on the system being classified high-risk.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] conditional-classification chain.

question: What responsible-AI principles must guide a Brazilian financial institution's AI systems under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 3 enumerates the principles that, with good faith, must guide AI development, implementation, and use: inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; self-determination and freedom of decision; human participation in the AI lifecycle and effective human oversight; non-discrimination; justice, equity, and inclusion; transparency, explainability, intelligibility, and auditability; reliability and robustness and information security; due process, contestability, and adversarial procedure; traceability of decisions for accountability; accountability, liability, and full reparation of damages; prevention, precaution, and mitigation of systemic risks; and non-maleficence and proportionality. Art. 2 adds foundations including the centrality of the human person and consumer protection. A financial institution must align its AI governance with these principles, which underpin the concrete obligations in Chapters II-IV.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] principle enumeration.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 address systemic or interdependency risks from AI systems in finance?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 addresses systemic risk principally through principle and classification criteria. Art. 3(XI) establishes prevention, precaution, and mitigation of systemic risks derived from intentional or unintentional uses and unforeseen effects of AI systems as a guiding principle. Art. 18(I) allows the competent authority to designate systems as high-risk based on large-scale implementation, considering the number of persons affected, geographic extent, duration, and frequency — a criterion relevant to interconnected financial AI. However, the bill does not establish a dedicated systemic-risk regime specific to finance (as, e.g., financial-stability regulators might); systemic concerns are handled through the principle, the Art. 18 designation criteria, and the impact-assessment consideration of the number of persons impacted (Art. 24(1)(c)).
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 require handling uncertainty in measuring AI risks?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 24(2) codifies the precautionary principle for measurement uncertainty: when using AI systems that may generate irreversible or hard-to-reverse impacts, the algorithmic impact assessment must also take into account incipient, incomplete, or speculative evidence (evidências incipientes, incompletas ou especulativas). This is reinforced by Art. 3(XI)'s principle of prevention, precaution, and mitigation of systemic risks. For a financial institution, this means uncertainty about a high-risk system's potential harms cannot be used to defer action; where impacts could be irreversible, the institution must weigh even preliminary or uncertain evidence in its risk assessment and mitigation decisions.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 24(2) precautionary wording.

question: How should a Brazilian bank treat risks in a fraud-detection AI that is not classified as high-risk under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Since fraud detection is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, a fraud-detection AI is subject to the baseline requirements rather than the enhanced high-risk regime. The provider must perform and document a preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13(2)). The general governance measures of Art. 19 apply (transparency, bias-mitigation data-management, data-protection legitimation, information security). Importantly, because a fraud system that blocks transactions produces effects on customers, the Chapter II rights apply: affected persons may contest decisions and request human review under Arts. 9-10 where the decision significantly affects their interests. So even without high-risk status, the bank must document a preliminary assessment, apply general governance measures, and honor contestation and human-review rights.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Non-high-risk but Chapter II rights attach.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 address privacy and data protection for AI systems, and how does it relate to the LGPD?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 integrates data protection with Brazil's LGPD (Lei nº 13.709/2018). Art. 5(VI) grants affected persons the right to privacy and protection of personal data under applicable legislation. Art. 19(IV) requires, as a general governance measure, legitimation of data processing in conformity with data-protection law, including privacy by design and by default and techniques minimizing personal-data use. Art. 9(1) guarantees the right to correction of incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated data and the right to request anonymization, blocking, or elimination of unnecessary or unlawfully processed data, expressly referencing Art. 18 of the LGPD. Text-and-data-mining involving personal data is subject to the LGPD (Art. 42(3)). For a financial institution, AI data governance must therefore satisfy both PL 2338's governance measures and the LGPD.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] LGPD cross-references (Art. 9(1), Art. 42(3)).

question: How does PL 2338/2023 treat generative AI used by a bank for customer-facing content?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not create a separate generative-AI risk tier in the way the EU AI Act creates GPAI-specific rules; generative AI is handled through the general framework. Providers of general-purpose AI must include the indicated purposes/applications in their preliminary assessment (Art. 13(1)). Transparency rights apply: affected persons have the right to prior information about interacting with an AI system (Art. 5(I)) and to the Art. 7 disclosures, including the automated character of the interaction, with easily recognizable icons/symbols where applicable (Art. 7(1)). If a generative system is used for a high-risk purpose (e.g., feeding credit decisions), the high-risk obligations attach via Art. 17. For customer-facing generative content that is not high-risk, the core duty is clear disclosure that the content/interaction is AI-generated, paralleling EU AI Act Art. 50.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. BR has no dedicated GPAI tier; contrast with EU Chapter V.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 ensure accountability and traceability for AI decisions in a financial institution?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 builds accountability from principle to concrete duty. Art. 3(IX) establishes traceability of decisions across the AI lifecycle as a means of accountability and attribution of responsibility to a natural or legal person, and Art. 3(X) establishes accountability, liability, and full reparation of damages. Operationally, Art. 20(II) requires high-risk systems to use automatic operation-logging tools enabling assessment of accuracy and robustness and detection of discriminatory potential — providing the audit trail for accountability. Art. 27 makes providers and operators liable for damages (strict liability for high-risk systems under Art. 27(1)). For a financial institution, accountability is ensured through lifecycle traceability, operational logging of high-risk systems, and the liability regime.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 expect governance resources to be allocated across AI systems of different risk?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 embeds proportionality so that governance effort scales with risk. Art. 3(XII) establishes proportionality between the methods employed and the legitimate purposes of the systems as a principle. Art. 30(2)(b) provides that a governance program should be adapted to the structure, scale, and volume of operations and to the system's harm potential. The bill's tiered structure concentrates the heaviest obligations — impact assessment (Art. 22), enhanced governance (Art. 20) — on high-risk systems, while lower-risk systems face only preliminary assessment and general governance (Arts. 13, 19). A financial institution should therefore allocate the bulk of its governance resources to high-risk systems such as credit scoring and recruitment.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 30(2)(b).

question: What incentives does PL 2338/2023 create for a strong internal AI risk culture?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 creates concrete incentives for good governance culture. Art. 30(3) provides that voluntary adherence to a code of good practice and governance can be considered an indicator of good faith and will be taken into account by the competent authority when applying administrative sanctions. Art. 36(1) lists dosimetry criteria for sanctions that reward good risk culture, including the agent's good faith (II), the reiterated and demonstrated adoption of internal mechanisms to minimize risks — including algorithmic impact assessment and effective implementation of an ethics code (VIII), the adoption of a good-practices and governance policy (IX), and prompt adoption of corrective measures (X). A strong internal AI risk culture thus directly mitigates potential penalties.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 36(1) dosimetry item numbering.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 classify an AI system used for algorithmic trading by a Brazilian securities firm?
ground_truth: Algorithmic trading AI is not enumerated among the high-risk purposes in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, so it is not automatically high-risk under the bill. The provider must nonetheless perform and document a preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13). The competent authority may designate it high-risk under Art. 18 if criteria such as large-scale implementation (Art. 18(I)), potential for material harm (Art. 18(III)), or systemic effect are met — plausible for high-frequency trading affecting market stability. Absent such designation, algorithmic trading is subject to general governance measures (Art. 19) and the principle of systemic-risk mitigation (Art. 3(XI)). This treatment resembles the EU and Korean frameworks, which likewise do not currently list algorithmic trading as high-risk/high-impact, leaving it to sectoral securities regulation.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Algorithmic trading not listed; Art. 18 designation possible.
